55: Patent ownership and assignment: whether the Asset Contribution Agreement transferred the '142 Patent from MD/Totco to NOV.
We affirm the district court’s conclusion that NOV lacks standing to assert the ’142 Patent because a plain reading of the ACA reveals that it did not transfer the ’142 Patent from MD/Totco to NOV.
367: Interpretation of patent cross-license and divestment rider scope, including whether the Alcatel license covered MGWs, whether Nokia Siemens Networks B.V. was a separately identifiable business, and whether LM Ericsson could grant retroactive sublicenses after patent expiration.
We reject, therefore, High Point's argument that LM Ericsson's contractual right to grant retroactive sublicenses to its subsidiaries was extinguished when the licensed patents expired in July 2011.
426: Whether Diamond, as assignee/licensee under the PATA and Ancillary Agreement, received all substantial rights in the patents-in-suit and so is a patentee under 35 U.S.C. § 281 able to sue alone; court held Diamond is not a patentee because Sanyo retained substantial rights (license to make/use/sell and significant control over enforcement and litigation).
Accordingly, we hold that Diamond is not a “patentee” under 35 U.S.C. § 281.
427: Effect of nunc pro tunc agreements executed after the district court decision: court held precedent (Alps South) bars considering them to confer retroactive patentee status.
Because neither the en banc court nor the Supreme Court has overruled Alps South, we reject Diamond’s argument.
512: Whether Orbis, a non-party to the patent license agreement (PLA), could recover fees from Buckhorn under the PLA's fee/indemnity provision as a party or third-party beneficiary; held it could not.
Orbis is not a party to the PLA. As described above, the PLA is an agreement between SAS and Buckhorn and requires Buckhorn to indemnify SAS under certain circumstances.
1270: Patent assignment and ownership: whether Dr. Lotan assigned his inventive rights to AngioScore under Section 9(a) of the Consulting Agreement. The court held Section 9(a) does not provide for assignment, and left the Section 9(b) assignment question for remand.
Contrary to the district court’s conclusion, § 9(a) does not provide for assignment of Dr. Lotan’s rights.
1472: Whether Mirowski Family Ventures, a non-signatory, is bound by the 1991 Agreement's fee-shifting provision as a result of the 2006 Tolling Agreement; held bound and liable for Medtronic's fees.
Therefore, the district court did not err in finding that Mirowski Family Ventures was bound by the fee shifting provision of the 1991 Agreement.
1473: Whether Guidant and Boston Scientific are also liable for Medtronic's attorney fees under the 1991 Agreement; held not liable because only the party giving notice of infringement is obligated to pay fees.
Therefore, the district court correctly concluded that only Mirowski Family Ventures is liable for Medtronic’s attorney fees.
1614: Patent ownership: NanoVapor's obligation-to-assign ownership theory was waived by its representation that inventorship would be dispositive, so the court did not decide it.

NanoVapor's clear representation that such a determination would be "ultimately most likely dispositive" of the inventorship issue is a waiver of any assertion of ownership of Nathan and Matheson's rights.
1877: Interpretation of the Amended License Agreement: Candella held exclusionary rights because Disney did not retain a right to license the patents through the Affiliate clause.
We hold that Candella had exclusionary rights to the Artificial Flame Technology when this suit was brought.
1942: Scope of the Most Favored Licensee provision of the PCRA; held that the MFL provision does not apply to the Patents-in-Suit, so no license is owed for them.
We conclude that the District Court did not err in finding the MFL Provision does not apply to the Patents-in-Suit.
1965: Whether the contract-damages award for post-expiration royalties violates the Brulotte rule; challenge rejected, so Bayer's license-based recovery stands.
No established law declares that result prohibited under the Brulotte rule.
2353: Enforceability of the Attachment B assignment agreement; plaintiff's unenforceable-contract claim dismissed, so PepsiCo's claimed patent rights upheld
We discern no error in the district court's dismissal of the unenforceable contract claim on these grounds.
2730: Whether Ariosa's breach-of-contract and covenant counterclaims, which depend on the scope of a license to the '794 patent under the supply agreement, fall within the arbitration clause or its exclusion for patent scope, infringement, and validity disputes; the court held they are not arbitrable and affirmed denial of the motion to compel arbitration.
We agree that Ariosa's counterclaims are not subject to arbitration.
3485: Interpretation of the scope of the IPG patent license (field-of-use definition) under Delaware contract law; the court held the license ambiguous, so extrinsic evidence must be considered on remand, and vacated summary judgment that the accused technology fell outside the license.
We hold that the license is ambiguous, and accordingly, we vacate the district court's grant of summary judgment and remand for further consideration in light of the extrinsic evidence.
3762: Scope of patent license: whether the Ciena license's Licensed Products definition covers AT&T's combined systems
The accused AT&T systems combine Ciena and Fujitsu products with other components and are thus Licensed Products within the meaning of the licenses.
3989: Patent ownership: the transfer agreement did not transfer all substantial rights in the asserted patents to Lone Star, so Lone Star is not the patentee and cannot sue in its own name under §281.
we agree with the district court that AMD did not transfer all substantial rights in the asserted patents.
4069: Patent license dispute: whether Infineon's termination of the patent license agreement was wrongful and the agreement remains in effect; court held MACOM likely to succeed on its wrongful termination claim under California implied covenant law.

We hold only that, on the record before it, the district court did not err in finding that MACOM could likely establish that its activity outside the Agreement's licensed Field of Use did not breach the Agreement's implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
4245: Whether Section 4 of the Propagation Agreement, an option to obtain a future license to commercialize patented WA 38 apple trees, is an unenforceable agreement to agree; the court held it unenforceable, rejecting Phytelligence's extrinsic-evidence and course-of-dealing arguments.
Thus, Section 4 is an unenforceable agreement to agree, even considering the extrinsic evidence in a light most favorable to Phytelligence.
4340: Ownership of Disputed U.S. Patents under NDA paragraph 5: SiOnyx granted sole ownership, Hamamatsu not entitled to co-ownership
We agree with SiOnyx that the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting SiOnyx sole ownership of the Disputed U.S. Patents.
4341: Ownership of Disputed Foreign Patents (Japanese applications and foreign counterparts): district court's denial of sole ownership to SiOnyx reversed
we conclude that the district court abused its discretion in declining to grant to SiOnyx sole ownership of Hamamatsu's Japanese applications and any foreign applications claiming priority therefrom.
4634: Enforcement of the settlement agreement's patent non-assertion covenant and permanent injunction; court held ULC complied and Sauder's breach claims failed
Once again, Sauder asks us to depart from the clear and unambiguous language of the settlement agreement to impose additional obligations on ULC. We decline to do so.
4808: Whether the sublicense survived termination of the Master License Agreement; the court held the Master Agreement is ambiguous and extrinsic evidence must be considered on remand.
On its face, the Master Agreement is ambiguous as to whether the sublicensee's rights survive the termination of the Master Agreement.
4809: Fraunhofer's theory that the sublicense itself was terminated by bankruptcy rejection and failure to elect under 11 U.S.C. 365(n)(1) was rejected.
This termination theory is without merit.
5106: Whether the Software Development Agreement automatically assigned, or obligated assignment of, patent rights in the inventions to JFAX; the court held the SDA can be read not to assign patent rights and must be construed in James's favor at this stage.
we cannot conclude that the SDA precludes Mr. James from retaining ownership rights in patents on his inventions—either as itself an assignment or as a contract to assign.
5107: Whether the hired-to-invent doctrine created an implied obligation to assign the patent rights to JFAX; the court held the doctrine did not defeat standing at this stage.
Accordingly, it was improper to dismiss the case under Rule 12(b)(1) for lack of standing based on the hired-to-invent principle.
5199: Interpretation of the MLA forum selection clause (governing law clause 13.4) to determine whether it covers PTAB challenges to licensed patents, a contract dispute over a patent license; the court held the clause encompassed the PTAB petitions, so Dodocase was likely to succeed on its breach claim.

We therefore affirm the district court's holding on the first preliminary injunction requirement that Dodocase was likely to succeed on the merits of its claim that MerchSource violated the forum selection clause of the MLA by filing the PTAB petitions.
5261: Contract interpretation of License Agreement Section 1.2(d): whether the West-Ward final judgment of noninfringement triggered early generic entry for Mylan
Section 1.2(d) clearly states that Mylan may launch its generic colchicine product following a Final Court Decision
5326: Constitutional takings challenge to retroactive application of IPR to pre-AIA patents; the court addressed it under the Fifth Amendment rather than patent ownership, so this is coded as X07 instead
we hold that the retroactive application of IPR proceedings to pre-AIA patents is not an unconstitutional taking under the Fifth Amendment.
5886: Whether Schwendimann was the patentee (owner by assignment) of the '845 application and patent at the time suit was filed, given the post-suit reformation of the Hand-Altered Copy assignment.
Accordingly, we find that the District Court did not err in concluding that (1) Ms. Schwendimann was a patentee at the time of her Complaint
6629: Patent ownership and assignment: whether the 'will assign', trust and quitclaim provisions of the employment agreement transferred co-owner Hsiun's interest in the '788 patent to Infochips and later to Advanced Video.

The quitclaim provision waives Ms. Hsiun's rights to interests in any patent rights that she assigned under the agreement. But, as no patent rights were ever assigned to Infochips, the quitclaim provision has no application.
7043: Contract interpretation of a merger clause in a 2007 settlement and license agreement, deciding whether it extinguished a 2006 covenant not to sue on the '915 patent (patent license and rights dispute).
The 2006 Covenant remains operable, and it bars Molon's suit against Nidec for infringement of the '915 patent.
7232: Breach of patent license agreement: court rejected Trans Ova's argument that its breaches were excused by XY's earlier material breach
We agree with the district court that a reasonable jury could have found that Trans Ova's breaches occurred before XY's breach based on the trial evidence.
7455: Co-owner joinder under 35 U.S.C. § 262 and whether AntennaSys can sue for infringement without co-owner Windmill (and GBS Positioner LLC) and whether an express or implied license from a co-owner bars the suit; court left these factual questions for remand.

On remand, the district court should resolve all factual issues pertaining to AntennaSys's ability to bring its patent infringement claim against AQYR, including: (1) whether Windmill waived the right to object to AntennaSys's failure to meet the § 262 prerequisite
7797: Patent licensing, assignment and ownership: whether bylaw 3.10 effected a present automatic assignment of the inventions to UM or only a promise to assign, so title passed to Omni.
We conclude that paragraph 1 of bylaw 3.10 is most naturally read as a statement of intended disposition and a promise of a potential future assignment, not as a present automatic transfer.
8077: BASF co-ownership under the MTEA of five patents (Group A patents and '541); no co-ownership verdict affirmed.
Under those standards, we affirm the verdict of no BASF co-ownership of five patents but reverse the verdict of BASF co-ownership of the '792 patent.
8078: BASF co-ownership of the '792 patent under the MTEA; jury verdict of co-ownership reversed, so CSIRO is sole owner.
we affirm the verdict of no BASF co-ownership of five patents but reverse the verdict of BASF co-ownership of the '792 patent.
8123: Whether USFRF, as exclusive licensee, held all substantial rights and is a patentee under 35 U.S.C. § 281 so it can sue without joining USF; court held USFRF is not a patentee and could not sue without USF.
we conclude that the district court did not err in holding that USFRF is not a patentee under § 281 and thus could not sue without patentee USF.
8269: Scope of patent license and whether post-termination infringement is barred; the license termination question was not decided and the summary judgment was vacated for post-December 31, 2018 conduct.
we vacate the summary judgment order insofar as it applies to conduct that occurred after the purported termination of the license agreement on December 31, 2018, and remand for further proceedings.
8534: Patent ownership and assignment: the court found Sgromo did not hold ownership of the '422, '440 and '298 patents, and that his purported assignments had no legal effect.
Sgromo did not hold ownership of any of the patents or trademarks when he asserted them.
8582: Royalty obligations under a patent royalty agreement after a Texas divisive merger allocated liability to a new subsidiary; court held Plastronics Socket remained liable for royalties on socket sales with H-Pins.
Plastronics Socket cannot divest itself of the obligation to pay royalties on sockets sold with H-Pins.
9044: Patent ownership: whether Universal had ownership rights to assert the '196 patent in the ITC investigation, based on a 2012 present-conveyance assignment from inventor Barnett.
On its face, the agreement language constitutes a present conveyance.
9225: Contract interpretation of Section 3.2 of the Wi-LAN/Intel license: term license does not extend perpetually to post-expiration Intel chipset sales, so summary judgment of no infringement reversed

Because section 3.2 unambiguously grants Intel a limited license that does not extend to Licensed Activities occurring after the expiration of the agreement, we reverse the district court's grant of summary judgment of no infringement.
9267: Scope of Meso's exclusive license under prong A of Section 2.1 of the 1995 license, as to '939 patent claim 33; court affirmed denial of JMOL and did not reach the '779 and '729 patents.
we affirm the district court's denial of JMOL regarding prong A with respect to '939 patent claim 33, and we do not reach Meso's rights under this prong
9385: Patent licensing: whether the Termination Agreement terminated the Fortress license under contract interpretation of the RSA and License Agreement
In sum, the only reasonable interpretation of "rights . . . which by their nature survive" is that those rights do not include a bare unexercised license.
9489: Interpretation of the license and settlement agreement's forum selection clause and no-challenge covenants; court held the clause did not bar IPR filings after the Covenant Period because the agreement allowed IPRs during it.

because the forum selection clause governs both during and after the Covenant Period, the clause cannot operate to prohibit the filing of IPRs after the Covenant Period if it allowed them during the Covenant Period.
9921: Enforceability of the July 24, 2020 settlement agreement (covenant not to sue and release on patent portfolio): meeting of the minds, intent to be bound, and definiteness under Indiana contract law; district court enforcement affirmed.
we fully agree with its larger conclusion that the parties reached a binding agreement to settle this litigation.
9922: Scope of the covenant not to sue on 'NeurOptics' pupillometer patent portfolio': the Federal Circuit vacated the district court's broader construction and held the term covers only the Two Asserted Patents and the Five Additional Patents.

While we conclude that the district court erred in its reading of "NeurOptics' pupillometer patent portfolio," we fully agree with its larger conclusion that the parties reached a binding agreement to settle this litigation.
10049: Patent license marking provision: whether failure to mark RectorSeal products made the license grant conditional, so that Hilti's products were unlicensed (construed as covenant, not condition).
We also construe the words employed in the License at ¶ 4.6 as words of covenant, not words of condition.
10228: Enforceability and scope of the settlement agreement's mutual release and covenant not to sue under the patent (contract dispute over the patent covenant); the court held the January 21 agreed definition of Covered Products controls and reversed the enforcement order.

We reverse the district court's order concerning the Covered Products term; hold that the parties reached an agreement regarding the term on January 21; and remand for the district court to enter an appropriate order utilizing the January 21 agreed definition of Covered Products.
10607: Specific performance requiring defendants to assign design patents and a utility patent application to Ms. Markell under the confidentiality agreement; denied for lack of nexus to the agreement.
We affirm the district court's denial of plaintiffs' request for specific performance.
10882: Scope of the employment assignment provisions: they do not reach post-employment inventions merely because pre-employment work contributed to them, so Bio-Rad does not co-own the patents.
the assignment duty is limited to subject matter that itself could be protected as intellectual property before the termination of employment
11312: Patent ownership and assignment: whether the 2007 Forbes assignment to America Connect covered the '761 continuation-in-part, so that Causam owns the '268 patent through the 2014 assignment.
Mr. Forbes had good title to the '268 patent when he assigned it to Causam, and Causam therefore owns the patent.
11314: Patent ownership under a 1990 invention assignment agreement (whether the TRW agreement's entirely-own-time exception removed the '211 patent from automatic assignment to TRW, so that Core Optical held title and standing). The court held the contract ambiguous and vacated summary judgment of non-ownership, leaving ownership unresolved.

We conclude that the 1990 invention agreement "is capable of more than one reasonable interpretation," so inquiry beyond the language of the contract is needed to "determine the ultimate construction to be placed on the ambiguous language."
11492: Whether the A&M-TexasLDPC license agreement terminated when TexasLDPC shifted to enforcement; court held it did not terminate, so TexasLDPC retains the license rights.
Therefore, we hold the Agreement did not terminate when TexasLDPC shifted to only enforcement.
11758: Whether the exclusive licensee Ridge had all substantial rights in the '084 patent and so was a patentee under 35 U.S.C. § 281 (ownership/assignment of patent rights).
Because the Agreement did not convey all substantial rights in the '084 patent to Ridge, Ridge is not a “patentee” under 35 U.S.C. § 281.
12414: Construction of the ETSI FRAND commitment as a contract: a party that made the commitment must first comply with its good-faith negotiation obligation before pursuing injunctive relief based on its SEPs, which the court held against Ericsson.

a party that has made an ETSI FRAND commitment must have complied with the commitment's obligation to negotiate in good faith over a license to its SEPs before it pursues injunctive relief based on those SEPs.
13128: Patent licensing, assignment and ownership: whether the 2006 Agreement transferred all patent rights to Nelson, so ASI had no rights to assign to AIT in 2012
The 2006 Agreement did convey all patent rights to Nelson.
14762: Patent ownership by assignment: Dr. Rasmussen's 2006 present assignment to Wright was self-executing and never reassigned back, so Rasmussen did not hold title to the asserted patents.
Dr. Rasmussen had no rights in the Asserted Patents to convey to Rasmussen in 2020.
